**Subject: Response to Deposit Deduction – Reference to Tenancy Agreement and Deposit Protection Rules**

Dear Mr Pell,

I am writing to formally respond to your recent email regarding the return of my deposit. I appreciate that the tenancy has now concluded and that I returned the keys on 31 August 2026. However, I am concerned about the amount you have proposed to deduct from the deposit and would like to clarify the matter in accordance with the terms of our tenancy agreement and the relevant deposit protection rules.

As per **Clause 4.3** of the tenancy agreement, you are entitled to deduct from the deposit the **reasonable cost** of making good any damage caused by me, with **fair wear and tear excepted**. The check-in inventory, dated 1 March 2023, recorded the living room walls as “magnolia, freshly painted, good condition”. The check-out report, dated 3 September 2026, noted “light scuffing to living room walls near sofa; two picture hook holes”.

Given the above, I believe that the scuffing and the two picture hook holes fall within the scope of **fair wear and tear**, particularly as they appear to be minor and not caused by any misuse or neglect on my part. I am prepared to accept a deduction of **£60** for the two picture hook holes, as that is a reasonable and proportionate cost for the repair of that specific issue. However, I do not accept the deduction of **£900** for “full redecoration of the flat”, as this is not supported by the evidence provided and appears to be an excessive and unfounded charge.

Furthermore, under **Clause 9.2**, I am required to leave the property in the same condition as at the start of the tenancy, with fair wear and tear excepted. I have taken all reasonable care in maintaining the property during the tenancy, and I have no intention of causing unnecessary damage. I believe that any deductions should be limited to actual and reasonable costs incurred due to damage beyond fair wear and tear.

I trust that you will reconsider your position in light of the above and agree to a fair and reasonable deduction. If not, I will be forced to escalate this matter to the **Deposit Protection Service (DPS)**, as required by **Clause 4.1**, and pursue the resolution of this issue in accordance with the law.

I look forward to your prompt and considered response.

Yours sincerely,  
**Ms Aisha Okafor**

**Ms Aisha Okafor**

**Subject: Re: Deposit and Repairs Following Tenancy Termination**

Dear Mr Pell,

I am writing to formally respond to your recent email regarding the return of the deposit and the proposed deductions.

As per the terms of our Assured Shorthold Tenancy Agreement (dated 1 March 2023), and in line with the Deposit Scheme Rules, I would like to clarify the matter of the deposit and the deductions you propose.

**Clause 4.1** of the tenancy agreement states that the deposit must be protected with the Deposit Protection Service (DPS), which it was, on 10 March 2023. **Clause 4.3** outlines that any deductions from the deposit must be for "reasonable costs of making good any damage caused by the Tenant, fair wear and tear excepted." Furthermore, **Clause 9.2** requires the Tenant to leave the property in the same condition as at the start of the tenancy, as recorded in the check-in inventory, with fair wear and tear excepted.

The check-in inventory, dated 1 March 2023, clearly records the living room walls as "magnolia, freshly painted, good condition." The check-out report, dated 3 September 2026, notes "light scuffing to living room walls near sofa; two picture hook holes." These are not indicative of significant damage, and the scuffing and hook holes appear to be minor and consistent with fair wear and tear.

I accept that the two picture hook holes may require some attention, and I am willing to accept a deduction of £60 for filling and touching up these areas. However, I do not agree with the proposed deduction of £900 for "full redecoration of the flat." This amount is not supported by the condition of the property as recorded in the check-out report and is not justified under the terms of the tenancy agreement or the Deposit Scheme Rules.

I kindly request that you provide a detailed breakdown of the costs you intend to deduct from the deposit, in accordance with the rules. If you are unable to do so, I will be forced to escalate this matter to the relevant housing authority or the Deposit Protection Service, as required under the scheme.

Please note that I am happy to discuss this further if you are willing to do so in a professional and constructive manner.

Yours sincerely,  
**Ms Aisha Okafor**

**Ms Aisha Okafor**  
[Your Address]  
[Date]

Mr Graham Pell  
[Landlord's Address]  
Flat 2, 14 Saxby Street, Leicester LE2 0ND

**Subject: Re: Deposit Refund and Repairs**

Dear Mr Pell,

I am writing to formally request a refund of the deposit in accordance with the terms of our Assured Shorthold Tenancy Agreement dated 1 March 2023, and in line with the statutory deposit protection rules.

As per Clause 4.1 of the Agreement, the deposit of £1,450 was protected with the Deposit Protection Service (DPS) on 10 March 2023, which is within the required 30-day period. Clause 4.3 of the Agreement allows the Landlord to deduct reasonable costs for damage caused by the Tenant, excluding fair wear and tear. Clause 9.2 requires the Property to be returned in the same condition as at the start of the tenancy, as recorded in the check-in inventory dated 1 March 2023.

The tenancy ended on 31 August 2026, and I returned the keys on that day. The check-out report dated 3 September 2026 notes light scuffing to the living room walls near the sofa and two picture hook holes. These are not considered fair wear and tear, as the walls were described in the check-in inventory as "magnolia, freshly painted, good condition."

I accept that there may be some minor repairs required, and I am willing to pay a reasonable amount for the two picture hook holes, which I understand you are proposing to charge £60 for. However, the claim of £900 for "full redecoration" is not supported by the facts or the terms of the Agreement. There is no evidence that the entire flat requires redecoration, and such a deduction would be unreasonable and not in line with the deposit scheme rules.

Under the deposit scheme rules, the Landlord must provide a detailed breakdown of any deductions and provide the Tenant with a statement of the deposit refund within 14 days of the end of the tenancy. I have not received such a statement, and I am concerned that the proposed deduction of £900 is not justified.

Therefore, I respectfully request that you provide a clear and itemised account of any deductions made from the deposit, and that you return the remaining balance in full and in accordance with the deposit scheme rules.

I trust that you will treat this matter with the seriousness it deserves and respond in a timely manner.

Yours sincerely,  
**Ms Aisha Okafor**
